readerTitle: Why Microsoft sold Word and Excel in one box
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Microsoft Office, iTunes) + 실제 연구 (Stigler 1963, Hsee 1998) + 가상 사례 (소프트웨어 애드온, 물류 회사) · 모든 가격 수치는 설명용
insight: 묶음 판매가 효과를 내는 이유는 할인 때문이 아니다. 고객마다 각 제품의 가치를 다르게 매기는데, 묶으면 그 차이가 상쇄된다.
misconception: 번들은 여러 개를 싸게 넘기는 할인 수단일 뿐이며, 많이 넣을수록 더 가치 있어 보인다.

factChecks.note: Office 출시 연도(Mac 1989, Windows 1990)와 첫 구성(Word, Excel, PowerPoint)을 Microsoft 공식 자료로 확인하세요. 현재 Microsoft 365 브랜드로 판매된다는 문구도 게시 직전 확인이 필요합니다.

2번·3번 카드 계산(가상 수치): 개별 $40 판매 시 Reports 100명×$40 = $4,000, Scheduling 100명×$40 = $4,000, 합계 $8,000. 개별 $10 판매 시 200명×$10×2 = $4,000. 번들 $50 판매 시 두 그룹 모두 가치 합계 $50이므로 200명×$50 = $10,000. 증가율 2,000 ÷ 8,000 = 25%. 추가 고객 1명당 비용은 0에 가깝다고 가정했습니다.
Stigler(1963)가 영화 블록 부킹을 고객별 가치 차이로 설명했다는 점, Adams & Yellen(1976)이 이를 일반화했다는 점을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
Hsee(1998) 식기 세트 실험: 온전한 24개 세트가 일부 깨진 조각이 섞인 40개 세트보다 따로 평가할 때 더 높게 평가됐다는 결과. 조각 수와 평가 방식을 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 금액을 쓰지 않았습니다.
iTunes Music Store 2003년 4월 출시, 곡당 99센트를 Apple 보도자료로 확인하세요. 앨범 판매 감소의 인과 관계는 단정하지 않고 일반적으로만 서술했습니다.

cards.title: Why Microsoft sold Word and Excel in one box
body: Around 1990, Microsoft started selling Word, Excel and PowerPoint together under one name: Office.
Plenty of buyers mainly needed just one of them. A writer lived in Word. An accountant lived in Excel. Yet the bundle outlived the boxed-software era and still sells today as Microsoft 365.

image.label: Three separate boxes merging into one box
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 각각 문서, 표, 슬라이드 아이콘이 그려진 작은 상자 세 개가 하나의 큰 상자로 합쳐지는 장면. 실제 Microsoft 로고나 제품 아이콘은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Two add-ons, two kinds of customers.
body: Your software sells two add-ons: Reports and Scheduling. You have 100 agencies and 100 clinics. Agencies would pay $40 a month for Reports but only $10 for Scheduling. Clinics are the opposite.
Extra customers cost you almost nothing. Which price earns the most each month?

options.feedback: Each group buys the add-on it loves, so you earn $8,000. But you leave the $10 each group would pay for the other add-on on the table.

options.text: Sell each add-on for $10 so everyone buys both
options.feedback: Everyone buys, but you earn only $4,000. You gave up the high value each group sees in its favorite.
Every customer values the pair at $50, so all 200 buy. You earn $10,000. Next card shows why.

cards.title: Same products, different totals.
body: The bundle earns **25% more** without changing either product. Each group values the add-ons differently, but both groups value the *pair* the same: $50.

breakdown.label: Each at $10
breakdown.detail: All 200 buy both, at a low price

breakdown.label: Each at $40
breakdown.detail: Each group buys only its favorite

cards.title: Bundling
body: **Bundling** means selling several products together for one price.

The key is not the discount. It's that customers disagree about what each part is worth. One loves A, another loves B. Priced alone, you must pick a high price and lose some buyers, or a low price and lose money from fans. Bundled, those differences **even out**, so one price fits far more people.

image.label: Two uneven bars that add up to equal totals
image.brief: 두 고객 그룹의 막대 그래프. 그룹 1은 "Reports $40 + Scheduling $10", 그룹 2는 "Reports $10 + Scheduling $40". 각 막대를 쌓으면 둘 다 "$50" 높이로 똑같아지는 모습을 강조.

cards.title: Economists spotted this in movie theaters.
body: In 1963, economist George Stigler studied why film studios sold movies to theaters in blocks rather than one by one. His answer: theaters valued each film differently, but the block's total value was more alike from theater to theater.
In 1976, William Adams and Janet Yellen showed the same logic works across many products.
Office fits the pattern. Writers and accountants rated Word and Excel very differently, but many valued the set similarly.

cards.title: Bundles can also come apart.
body: You can sell only the bundle (*pure bundling*) or the bundle plus each part on its own (*mixed bundling*). Mixed bundling keeps customers who truly want just one item.

Unbundling happens too. When the iTunes Music Store launched in 2003, songs sold for 99 cents each. Fans of one hit no longer had to buy a whole album. When buyers can easily pick only what they want, a bundle stops working as well.

cards.title: More stuff is not more value.
body: Bundling works best when each extra unit costs you little, like software. With physical goods, every item you add has a real cost, so throwing in things nobody values just lowers your margin.

Filler can also backfire. In a 1998 study by Christopher Hsee, people judged a complete 24-piece dinnerware set more valuable than a 40-piece set that included some broken pieces. Weak items can drag down the whole bundle.

cards.title: Now it's a logistics company.
body: You run a warehouse that also delivers. Online shops care most about fast delivery and see storage as a small extra. Wholesalers have their own trucks and mostly want storage.

options.feedback: Online shops may like it, but wholesalers with their own trucks won't pay for delivery they never use. You could lose them entirely.

options.text: Offer the package at a good price, and keep storage and delivery available separately
options.feedback: Customers who value both get a deal that pulls them in, and those who want one part still buy. You gain bundle sales without driving anyone away.

options.text: Keep pricing storage and delivery separately
options.feedback: Simple and safe, but you miss customers who would pay a bit more to get both from one partner.

cards.title: Bundle where customers disagree about the parts.
body: A bundle earns more when different buyers love different pieces, and the extras cost you little to add.
**Try it today:** pick two things you sell. Write down which customers value each one most. If they are different people, sketch a bundle and keep the single items too.
